source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles. Artificial Intelligence 32(1):57-95
finding: Founding paper. Diagnosis uses only the system description (structure and intended behaviour) and the observation. No fault statistics or expert rules. Contrasts this with the experiential approach (MYCIN).
numbers: Pages 57-95. Defines system (SD, COMPONENTS), observation OBS, abnormality predicate AB.
quote: A diagnosis is a conjecture that some minimal set of components are faulty.
limits: First-order logic assumed; consistency is undecidable in general, so a sound and complete theorem prover is assumed. Only a theory and an algorithm, no empirical test.
agent_relevance: Our agent can treat the model as a code artefact and let a checker, not the language model, decide consistency. Matches the guardrail that code decides transitions.

source: Reiter (1987) Definition 2.4 and the Principle of Parsimony
finding: A diagnosis is a subset-minimal set A of components such that SD + OBS + {AB(c) for c in A} + {not AB(c) for the rest} is consistent. Minimality (not minimum cardinality) is the parsimony rule.
numbers: Full adder example (Fig 1: 2 XOR, 2 AND, 1 OR gates). Inputs 1,0,1 gave outputs 1,0; both outputs wrong. Three diagnoses: {X1}, {X2,O1}, {X2,A2}.
limits: Minimal is not the same as most probable. Parsimony can hide a real multi-fault case, and supersets of a diagnosis are not always diagnoses (de Kleer, Mackworth, Reiter 1992).
agent_relevance: Gives a precise, checkable definition of 'smallest set of broken parts consistent with all evidence'. Usable as the ranking rule of a code-run reasoner.

source: Reiter (1987) Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5: diagnoses are minimal hitting sets of conflict sets
finding: A set is a diagnosis iff it is a minimal hitting set of the collection of (minimal) conflict sets. A conflict set is a set of components that cannot all be normal given the observation.
numbers: Adder: minimal conflict sets {X1,X2} and {X1,A2,O1}; minimal hitting sets {X1}, {X2,A2}, {X2,O1}.
limits: Needs conflict sets from a theorem prover. Computing a further minimal diagnosis is NP-hard in general (Rodler 2020 footnote).
agent_relevance: This is the core algorithm: find conflicts with a checker, then hit them. A conflict is just a failed check naming the guilty items. Our 'revise only from real output' guardrail is the same idea.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 4.2: HS-tree algorithm and pruning rules
finding: Builds a breadth-first tree. Each node is labelled with a conflict set; each edge removes one suspected component. Three devices: reuse labels, close nodes whose path set contains a known hitting set, prune redundant edges. Each saves calls to the expensive prover.
numbers: Worked example Fig 2-3 with F = {{2,4,5},{1,2,3},{1,3,5},...}. Breadth first returns minimum-cardinality diagnoses first.
limits: Algorithm as printed was wrong (Greiner et al. 1989). Breadth-first needs memory exponential in diagnosis size.
agent_relevance: A concrete small algorithm a code harness can run. The cost model 'number of prover calls' maps to number of model or tool calls.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 5: measurements, Theorem 5.7 and Corollary 5.9
finding: A new measurement keeps old diagnoses that predicted the value and drops those that predicted another value, but can add new multiple-fault diagnoses. Divide and conquer is justified only among single-fault diagnoses (Corollary 5.9).
numbers: Example 5.10 (multiplier/adder device): measuring out(M1)=6 left {A1} as the only single fault; remaining diagnoses {A1}, {M2,M3}, {M2,A2}.
limits: Reiter only poses the measurement-selection problem; he gives no selection rule (that is GDE). He leaves open how to reuse the pruned tree after a measurement.
agent_relevance: Warning for the agent: a probe that rules out the leading suspect can reveal new double-fault hypotheses. Do not treat 'suspect eliminated' as 'problem localised'.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 6-7: default logic link, generalisation beyond first-order logic, relation to de Kleer and Williams
finding: Diagnoses correspond to extensions of a default theory (Theorem 6.1) whose defaults say 'assume each component normal unless shown otherwise'. Diagnostic reasoning is nonmonotonic: new observations can retract earlier conclusions. Reiter notes de Kleer and Williams reached the same characterisation independently.
numbers: Theorem 6.1: extensions equal the sentences predicted by a diagnosis.
quote: it is based upon an unformalized approach to diagnosis, while our results have been derived from initial formal definitions
limits: Reiter's own priority claim: their result rests on an unformalized approach; his is derived from formal definitions.
agent_relevance: Supports a belief store that is revisable by design: default 'normal' assumptions retracted only on a conflict signal (guardrail G1: doubt only on a signal).

source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis. Artificial Intelligence 41
finding: Reiter's pruned HS-tree can lose minimal hitting sets, hence lose diagnoses. The bug comes from combining the node-closing rules with the redundant-edge pruning rule. Fix: build a directed acyclic graph (HS-DAG) that reuses nodes and relabels pruned nodes.
numbers: Counterexample collection {{a,b},{b,c},{a,c},{b,d},{b}}: the minimal hitting set {a,b} is missed by the original tree. Second example {{a,b},{a},{b}} shows the need for relabelling.
quote: Reiter's description of the algorithm is incorrect in that some diagnoses can be missed under certain conditions.
limits: A correctness fix, not an empirical test. The fix works with non-minimal conflict sets too; de Kleer and Williams require minimal ones.
agent_relevance: A published correctness error in a famous 1987 algorithm. Lesson: have code test the reasoner against brute force before trusting it.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults. Artificial Intelligence 32(1):97-130 (2008 corrected reprint)
finding: GDE (General Diagnostic Engine). Separates behaviour prediction from diagnosis. Uses an ATMS to record which assumptions each prediction depends on. Conflicts are minimal sets of assumptions that cannot all hold; candidates are minimal sets that hit every conflict. The candidate space is kept as minimal candidates, not all 2^n.
numbers: Fig 2 circuit (3 multipliers M1-M3, 2 adders A1-A2). Initial candidate space 2^5 = 32. Observation F=10 (expected 12) gives conflict {A1,M1,M2}; after G=12 the candidates are [A1], [M1], [A2,M2], [M2,M3].
limits: Tested on 'many examples' of digital circuits; no systematic benchmark table in this paper. Assumes independent faults, that measuring does not disturb the device, and incomplete constraint propagation.
agent_relevance: Gives the incremental pattern: keep a minimal set of hypotheses and update it on each new check. A template for a code-run candidate list.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Section 4: minimum-entropy measurement selection
finding: Next probe = the one with lowest expected entropy of the candidate distribution. Needs only prior failure probabilities of single components. Candidate probabilities come from Bayes rule and independence of faults. With no symptom yet, every probe has expected cost near 1, so nothing is gained until a symptom appears.
numbers: Cascaded inverters, p(fail)=.01, a=1 known: costs b .98, c .96, d .94, e .93 (far end is best). After e=0: best probe c (.31). With p(A)=.025 and a=1, e=1: b .975 beats c .992. Fig 2 with p=.01 and m=16: initial P(no fault)=.951; after F=10 the three single faults [A1], [M1], [M2] each have .323.
limits: Probability that a candidate predicts no value is approximated with 1/m; the paper itself calls this estimate suspect. Needs priors that are often unknown.
agent_relevance: An information-gain rule for 'which check next' that a program can compute, instead of asking the model what to try.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Section 6 discussion: comparison with SOPHIE, DART, Davis, and complexity claims
finding: Claims earlier work (Davis, SOPHIE, LOCAL, DART) assumed a single fault and used ad hoc half-split probing. GDE handles any number of faults. Claims the minimal-candidate representation grows roughly with the square or cube of the number of components in practice, not exponentially.
numbers: Claim (authors, no table): 'in practice our approach tends to grow with the square or cube of the number of potential faults.' Worst case still exponential.
limits: Author claims with no measured scaling table. Later work (Feldman 2010) shows exact algorithms degrade with fault cardinality.
agent_relevance: Half-split is the single-fault special case of entropy probing. The single-fault assumption is what the older heuristics lose.

source: de Kleer (1990) Using crude probability estimates to guide diagnosis. Artificial Intelligence 45(3):381-391
finding: If faults are independent, rare and equally likely, the entropy rule reduces to a score S(x) = sum over outcomes of c_k ln c_k, where c_k is the number of smallest-size diagnoses predicting value k. Lower is better. No numeric priors needed.
numbers: Four buffers in series, input 1, output 0: single faults [A],[B],[C],[D]. Score for probe X = 3 ln 3 + 1 ln 1 = 3.3, worse than a probe that splits the diagnoses evenly.
limits: Needs the equal-and-small probability assumption; can be generalised to groups of components with different rates.
agent_relevance: A cheap, prior-free rule for a code-run probe chooser: pick the check that splits the live hypotheses most evenly. Reproduces half-split without assuming one fault.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1989) Diagnosis with behavioral modes (Sherlock). IJCAI-89
finding: Sherlock gives every component a set of behavioural modes (ok, known faults, and an 'unknown' mode that predicts nothing and so never conflicts). Fault models sharpen discrimination and probe choice, while the unknown mode keeps unforeseen faults diagnosable.
numbers: Tested on circuits from a 3-inverter example up to ALUs of 400 gates with 4 behavioural modes each. Example: p(ok) about .918, stuck-at modes small, unknown mode about .027.
limits: Fault modes make the candidate space combinatorial; Sherlock uses focusing and probability cut-offs. No timing table in the text I read.
agent_relevance: The 'unknown mode' is a safe place for the agent to put 'I have no model of how this part fails', so ignorance does not create false conflicts.

source: de Kleer, Mackworth, Reiter (1992) Characterizing diagnoses and systems. Artificial Intelligence 56(2-3)
finding: Shows that not every superset of a diagnosis need be a diagnosis, so minimal diagnoses alone do not characterise all diagnoses. Introduces kernel diagnoses as an alternative, and a restriction on the axioms (weak fault models) under which minimal diagnoses suffice.
numbers: Theorems 2-12 on conflicts, implicants and kernel diagnoses (scan is badly OCR'd; I read the abstract and structure only).
limits: Heavy OCR errors. I could not check individual theorems.
agent_relevance: Minimal explanation is safe only when the model says nothing about how parts fail (weak-fault models). Use weak models as the default.

source: Davis and Genesereth structure-based diagnosis, as described in de Kleer and Williams (1987) and Reiter (1987)
finding: Davis's constraint-suspension and Genesereth's design-description approach started the model-based line. The obvious extension of Davis's method to multiple faults is exponential (de Kleer and Williams's description). SOPHIE used half-split probing built on a single-fault presupposition.
numbers: No new numbers; secondary description only.
limits: Original Davis (1984) and Genesereth (1984) papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Historic baseline: the older 'cut the system in half' method is a special case.

source: Bylander, Allemang, Tanner, Josephson (1991) complexity of abduction/diagnosis, as stated in Feldman et al. (2010)
finding: Deciding whether a diagnosis with at most k faults exists is NP-hard for arbitrary propositional models. Computing all diagnoses is harder, since there can be exponentially many.
numbers: Result stated in Feldman et al. 2010 introduction; also cites Friedrich, Gottlob, Nejdl 1990.
limits: Secondary citation; the original Bylander paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A hard limit: do not promise exact full enumeration on large models; budget it and report partial results.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) Approximate model-based diagnosis using greedy stochastic search (SAFARI). JAIR 38:371-413
finding: Greedy stochastic search that gives up the guarantee of minimality for speed. For weak-fault models it finds a subset-minimal diagnosis in polynomial time using only unit propagation. At least one order of magnitude faster than the deterministic algorithms CDA and HA on multiple faults, and works at fault cardinalities where they fail.
numbers: Benchmarks: 74XXX and ISCAS85 circuits (c432 to c7552). SAFARI found a diagnosis for every observation vector; deterministic algorithms degraded with model size and fault cardinality. It reached minimal-cardinality diagnoses in 78-100% of cases (weak and strong fault models) for N up to 27,770 runs; failures at most 13.55%, mostly where only one single-fault diagnosis exists.
limits: No minimal-cardinality guarantee. Quality fell for strong-fault models from c3540 upwards. An SLS MaxSAT competitor often returned no diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Anytime behaviour: it always returns some diagnosis. A good fit for a budgeted agent loop.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) A model-based active testing approach to sequential diagnosis (FRACTAL). JAIR 39:301-334
finding: Adds control inputs so the diagnoser can choose test vectors, not only probe internal nodes. Compares FractalG (greedy), FractalATPG (test pattern generation) and FractalP (probing baseline). The number of remaining minimum-cardinality diagnoses decays geometrically as a few inputs become controls.
numbers: ISCAS85/74XXX circuits with cone reduction. Correlation of estimated with true expected remaining diagnoses for reduced c880: min .834, max 1, avg .972. Cites one-step lookahead as optimal under unit test costs and equal priors (Pattipati and Alexandridis 1990).
limits: Uses minimum-cardinality diagnoses as the hypothesis set. Active testing is NP-hard in the worst case.
agent_relevance: Models 'run a discriminating test' as an explicit optimisation over test inputs, which a code harness can do.

source: Grastien, Haslum, Thiebaux (2023) A more general theory of diagnosis from first principles. arXiv:2309.16180
finding: Generalises Reiter to dynamic systems and any preference order over hypotheses. Algorithms: preferred-first (like Reiter) and preferred-last. A test solver checks whether a set of hypotheses intersects the diagnosis. Conflicts become sets of diagnostic properties, not component sets.
numbers: Power-network alarm benchmark: 129 instances, 2-146 alarms, 2-104 relevant components, components with up to 1,024 states. Junction-tree method solved only 23 of 129. SAT-based preferred-first solved the most; instances it failed were solved by no other method. BDD solved 4 to 12 fewer than the preferred-first variants.
limits: Discrete-event focus. Hypothesis spaces of sequences are harder than sets.
agent_relevance: Shows the Reiter loop (test, get conflict, refine) still beats enumerating every explanation in 2023 on real data.

source: Ignatiev, Morgado, Marques-Silva (2017) Model based diagnosis of multiple observations with implicit hitting sets. arXiv:1707.01972
finding: Analysing many failing observations one at a time can be infeasible and does not give a diagnosis consistent with all of them. An implicit-hitting-set method (the modern form of Reiter's idea, with MaxSAT) analyses all together.
numbers: ISCAS85 scenarios: their method (DEx) computed the correct diagnosis for all 1,140 benchmarks. With separate analysis (LBX, RS), the share of diagnoses computed dropped quickly and was 0% for most instances.
limits: Circuit benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: Evidence for pooling all failing checks into one problem rather than fixing one failure at a time.

source: Rodler (2016) Interactive debugging of knowledge bases. arXiv:1605.05950 (PhD thesis)
finding: Applies Reiter's HS-tree plus QuickXplain (conflict finder) to debugging ontologies. Adds probability-weighted best-first search and entropy-based query selection so a user is asked as few questions as possible. With n equally split diagnoses the ideal is log2 n queries.
numbers: Real ontologies: under 10 minimal conflict sets of at most 13 elements; minimal diagnoses of cardinality up to 9. Entropy query selection beat 'split-in-half' and random by more than 50% when diagnoses had cardinality 2; about 8 s to produce one query.
limits: Simulated users on benchmark ontologies. Entropy selection depends on prior fault probabilities; the thesis tests extreme, moderate and uniform priors and proposes a hybrid (RIO) for poor priors.
agent_relevance: Closest worked example of an interactive diagnoser that asks the fewest informative questions. Maps to an agent asking a tool or user the most splitting question.

source: Rodler (2020; AIJ 2022) Sound, complete, linear-space, best-first diagnosis search (RBF-HS). arXiv:2009.12190
finding: Replaces Reiter's HS-Tree with a recursive best-first search so memory is linear while soundness, completeness and best-first order stay. Needed because HS-Tree needs exponential memory.
numbers: Twelve knowledge-base debugging problems, ld in {2,6,10,20} diagnoses per iteration. Memory savings up to 98%; HS-Tree used up to about 49 times more memory, at similar or lower time cost.
limits: Minimum-cardinality setting; knowledge-base debugging cases, not circuits.
agent_relevance: Memory is a real constraint of Reiter's algorithm; relevant if an agent's candidate list lives in a bounded context window.

source: Rodler and Elichanova (2020; AAAI 2022) Do we really sample right in model-based diagnosis? arXiv:2009.12178
finding: Tests the long-standing habit of estimating from the k most probable diagnoses (a biased sample) when choosing the next measurement. Random samples give better estimates, but best-first samples can still need fewer measurements for some heuristics.
numbers: Median correlation of estimate with truth (best-first sample, worst-first sample) for k = 6, 10, 20, 50 started (0.76, 0.5), (0.83, 0.52), (0.95, 0.7), then 0.98 for best-first at k = 50. Best-first needed the fewest measurements overall and for heuristics ENT and SPL with small samples; it was worst for heuristic MPS.
limits: Knowledge-base debugging data set; assumed measurement times (1 min, 10 min) change the ranking. Better theory did not always mean better practice (RQ5).
agent_relevance: If the agent keeps only its top few hypotheses to decide what to check next, expect bias; keep one random lower-ranked hypothesis in the sample.

source: Orvalho, Janota, Manquinho (2024; v2 2025) CFaults: model-based diagnosis for fault localization in C programs with multiple test cases. arXiv:2407.09337
finding: Programs are treated as circuits and statements as components. All failing tests go into one MaxSAT formula, so every returned diagnosis is consistent with every failing test and is subset-minimal.
numbers: TCAS (41 programs): CFaults 41 of 41 valid (100%), BugAssist 41 of 41, SNIPER 7 of 41 (17.07%, 34 memouts). C-Pack-IPAs (486 programs): CFaults 483 (99.38%), BugAssist 454 (93.42%), SNIPER 446 (91.77%). Timeout 3600 s, 32 GB.
limits: Two small C benchmark sets; no LLM involved. The refinement step costs a little time.
agent_relevance: Direct bridge to code debugging: a code-run reasoner can use MBD on programs, not only circuits.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Model-based diagnosis: automating end-to-end diagnosis of network failures (NetDx). arXiv:2506.23083
finding: Derives diagnosis procedures from a model of packet forwarding and routing, from user-level symptoms to root cause, across data and control plane.
numbers: Automated fault injection: 100% of injected faults diagnosed correctly. Of 33 real cloud-provider faults inside its domain, 30 (91%) were diagnosed in seconds instead of hours.
limits: Proof of concept on an emulated P4 network. The 33 faults were already selected as in-domain.
agent_relevance: MBD works on a live engineering domain in 2025 when the model is hand-built and a solver does the reasoning.

source: McCabe, Lukens, Huang (2026) Can LLM agents efficiently identify appliance faults? CoffeeBench. arXiv:2610.19291
finding: A simulated espresso machine with interacting components and failure modes, exposed through sensors and actions via an MCP server. Twelve models tested. LLMs struggle to identify faults from sensors alone, but the best refine the fault options over turns. Some models do no better than guessing with elimination.
numbers: One-turn accuracy (pass^1): Gemini 2.5 Pro 61.1%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 56.8%, Claude 4.5 Sonnet 56.8%; only one model above 60%; three models roughly as poor as or worse than a guess-and-eliminate baseline. An explicit episode-state tracker cut timeouts to under 8% and brought Nemotron 120B level with Claude 4.5 Haiku. High initial uncertainty meant over 97% more turns; judged soundness of explanation was over 24% higher on successful turns.
limits: One simulated appliance. The agent had no explicit structural model, so this is a baseline for what MBD would replace, not a test of MBD.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap an explicit model plus a code-kept candidate set could close: weak models failed at tracking which options were already eliminated, which a hitting-set bookkeeper does for free.

source: Vaccarino et al. (2026) Repairing LLM-generated specifications with deterministic diagnosis (DRAGO). arXiv:2610.22568
finding: Replaces LLM self-critique of generated formal specs with deterministic diagnosis (contract checks, solver probes in the spirit of deletion-based minimal-unsatisfiable-subset extraction, alignment checks). A rewrite is accepted only if the diagnosed error weight strictly falls.
numbers: Five benchmarks, four models, three formalisms. LLM-diagnostic repair broke 11.8% of initially correct artifacts (1,006 of 8,559); DRAGO broke 1.3% (110 of 8,528). Accuracy +12.9 points over zero-shot and +8.7 over LLM-diagnostic repair. PDDL: DRAGO 104 wrong-to-right vs 12 regressions; self-review 159 fixes vs 254 breaks.
limits: Uses MUS-style conflict finding, not Reiter's full hitting-set tree. A benchmark defect caps PDDL accuracy near 80.7%.
agent_relevance: Measured support for our rule that revisions must cite real, code-found output, and for accepting a revision only when a count goes down.

source: Nakos and Forbus (2024) Interactively diagnosing errors in a semantic parser. arXiv:2407.06400
finding: Casts symptom identification and error localisation in a hand-built semantic parser (CNLU) as GDE-style model-based diagnosis, asking the user natural-language questions.
numbers: Work in progress, demonstrated on synthetic examples only; no accuracy numbers.
limits: Completeness assumptions ('one of these is right') are weak and cause no conflicts, so they do not drive GDE. The authors flag this as a design challenge.
agent_relevance: A 2024 use of GDE for debugging a language system. Warns that weak 'one of these' assumptions give no conflict signal.

source: Matei et al. (2026) Ambiguity detection and elimination in automated executable process modeling. arXiv:2604.10884
finding: Uses model-based diagnosis to trace disagreement between LLM-generated process models back to ambiguous policy text, then repairs the text and regenerates.
numbers: After repair of one policy text, over 90% of regenerated models gave the same outcome; for a second policy about 70% did.
limits: Two case policies, no controlled baseline; measures agreement among generated models, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Agreement among samples is a symptom, and MBD finds which clause causes it; consistent with reading agreement as a hint, not proof (guardrail G4).

source: Shi, Yang, Chen (2026) From finding to fixing: how useful is fault localization for agentic program repair? arXiv:2610.25826
finding: Six recent fault-localisation methods tested with LLM repair agents on SWE-bench Verified and Defects4J, three LLMs, 16,248 trajectories. FL does not consistently raise repair success, and higher localisation accuracy does not consistently give larger gains.
numbers: Accurate locations cut repair token use by up to 39.2%, but current FL methods often cost more tokens than they save. Adding bug causes to locations raised repair success further.
limits: FL methods tested are mostly LLM or spectrum based, not formal MBD. Abstract and introduction read; body skimmed.
agent_relevance: Caution: locating the faulty part does not by itself raise repair success. Pair localisation with a cause and a real check.

source: He and Apostolaki (2026) Let AI agents translate networks, not reason about them (TypoNet). arXiv:2607.22947
finding: Position paper. An LLM translates network artefacts into symbolic rules; a solver reasons. An adversarial 'Detractor' raises counterexamples to rules. A specialised fault-to-symptom theory given to an agent as a tool improved localisation F1 for every LLM tested.
numbers: Foundation theory: 128 rules, 3 h and $18.6 one-time cost, 97.4% held-out agreement with ground truth; disabling the Detractor dropped agreement to 41%; 48 of 50 planted wrong rules caught; 118 of 128 (92%) of rules reused unchanged on a network twice the size. Sonnet 4.6 with TypoNet reached F1 0.83 on the hardest incidents.
limits: Preprint on an emulated WAN. Figure text was garbled in extraction, so some model-by-model numbers could not be checked.
agent_relevance: Same split as our design: the model writes the model, code reasons over it. The ablation is a direct number on why adversarial model checking matters.

source: Rodler (2023) Don't treat the symptom, find the cause! Efficient AI methods for (interactive) debugging. arXiv:2306.12850
finding: Habilitation thesis that introduces model-based diagnosis and its open challenges. Known only from an arXiv listing summary; body not read.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; listing text only.
agent_relevance: Pointer for a deeper review of interactive MBD in a later pass.
